analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to verify a homebuyer can afford the mortgage and restricts risky loan fees and practices.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2007 with 26 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to require mortgage lenders and brokers to verify — with real documentation like tax returns and pay stubs — that a borrower can afford the full cost of a home loan, including taxes, insurance, and the higher payments that come when an adjustable rate resets. It would also ban prepayment penalties on adjustable-rate mortgages, ban steering borrowers into worse loans than they qualify for, cap financed points and fees at 5% of the loan, and make mortgage brokers legally owe a duty to act in the borrower's best interest. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners, especially people taking out adjustable-rate or low-documentation loans, gain the most: a lender would have to prove they can afford the loan after the rate resets, they could not be steered into a worse loan than they qualify for, they could refinance without a prepayment penalty, and rolled-in fees would be capped at 5% of the loan. Borrowers using mortgage brokers would gain a legal right to a broker who works for them, not for the lender. Holders of below-market government or nonprofit mortgages would get counseling before refinancing out of them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders and brokers to verify — with tax returns, pay stubs, or bank records, not just the borrower's word — that a homebuyer can afford the full payments, including taxes, insurance, and mortgage insurance, and for adjustable-rate loans to afford the payment at the fully indexed rate plus 2%.
Bans prepayment penalties on adjustable-rate mortgages (except large 'jumbo' loans), so homeowners can refinance out of a bad loan without paying a fee.

Prohibits steering — putting a borrower into a worse loan than they qualify for — and caps financed points, finance charges, and fees at 5% of the loan principal, with broker compensation from any source counted in that cap.

Makes mortgage brokers legally owe a duty to act in the borrower's best interest, disclose all material facts, and accept no undisclosed compensation — the same fiduciary standard that applies to agents in other fields.

Requires independent counseling, verified by a certified nonprofit counselor, before a borrower refinances out of a below-market or income-based 'special mortgage' from a government or nonprofit program — protecting affordable-loan holders from being refinanced into worse terms.
Gives borrowers a private right to sue, treating the loan fees as actual damages when a broker violates the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and lenders pay: brokers would face new fiduciary duties, a cap on total compensation, disclosure rules, and a $500,000 net worth or $50,000 bond requirement that would squeeze out smaller shops; lenders would have to document borrower income and forgo prepayment penalties and fee-heavy loan structures on adjustable-rate mortgages. Borrowers with thin or hard-to-verify income could face slightly slower or harder-to-get loans as a result of stricter underwriting.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a hard 5% cap on financed points, charges, and fees with no adjustment for loan size or market conditions, which could push some costs into the interest rate or make small-dollar loans uneconomical for lenders to offer.

The minimum financial requirements — a $500,000 net worth or a $50,000 bond — would force many small or newly formed mortgage brokerages out of business, reducing competition and possibly making it harder for some borrowers, including first-time buyers, to find a broker.

Requiring verified income documentation and counseling before refinancing a subsidized or nonprofit 'special mortgage' adds paperwork, cost, and delay to transactions that are often time-sensitive for distressed borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were large and the costs modest and targeted. Requiring lenders to verify that a borrower can actually afford a mortgage — including taxes and insurance, and including the higher payment after an introductory rate resets — would have screened out the loans most likely to end in foreclosure. Banning prepayment penalties and steering, capping rolled-in fees, and making brokers legally answerable to the borrower are standard protections; the Dodd-Frank rules adopted years later are similar in design. The main costs fall on brokers and lenders who profited from fee-heavy, hard-to-repay loans, and there are real tradeoffs: tighter underwriting can make credit slower and harder to get for some lower-income borrowers, and the capital requirements would push small brokerages out. On balance, given the scale of foreclosure losses that followed, the protections outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on July 18, 2007, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the referral was the last official step the bill ever took.
Twenty-six House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats, but cosponsorship never translated into committee action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

The bill's core requirement — that lenders verify a borrower's ability to repay before making a home loan — anticipated the standards Congress later wrote into federal law after the financial crisis, but this bill itself never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers and lenders came out ahead: none of the bill's underwriting, fee, or fiduciary requirements ever took effect, and homeowners continued to bear the losses of the lending practices the bill targeted.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 18, 2007, with eight original cosponsors.

for.name: 26 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Clay, Cleaver, Johnson of Georgia, Lee, McCollum, Oberstar, Walz, and Woolsey as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral; the committee took no recorded action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 26 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Republican sponsor signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so the full partisan split on the substance was never recorded; no Republican supported it on paper.

industries.note: The bill would cap broker compensation within a 5% fee limit, ban steering borrowers into worse loans, impose a legal duty to act in the borrower's best interest, and require $500,000 in net worth or a $50,000 bond to stay in business. Brokers' existing business model — collecting fees and yield-spread payments from lenders regardless of whether the loan serves the borrower — would not survive as-is.

Ability-to-repay verification, a ban on prepayment penalties for adjustable-rate loans, and private lawsuits treating loan fees as damages would eliminate the riskiest and most profitable origination practices of the mid-2000s, including no-documentation loans that defaulted at high rates.
The bill would route refinancing of subsidized or nonprofit mortgages through certified independent counselors, creating a formal, required role for nonprofit counseling organizations.
